title: Star-Birth “Fireworks”
caption: Jets from the young star cluster HH 24, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/B. Reipurth, C. Aspin & T. Rector

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: At least six jets of gas shoot out of the reddish Herbig-Haro 24 complex in this Gemini North image, moving at supersonic speeds. HH 24 is a small cluster of young stars buried in a molecular cloud in the direction of Orion. The region holds the highest concentration of jets known anywhere, and this is described as the most detailed view of it ever obtained from the ground.

One jet is badly disturbed, which suggests its source may be a close binary star whose orbit jostles the jet. Most puzzling are five very-low-mass protostars sitting well outside the cloud's core, where the gas is far too thin for stars to have formed.

Astronomers think these orphans were most likely flung out soon after birth from the core, home to a small multiple protostellar system called SSV 63. Such ejections may happen when crowded young stars begin moving around one another chaotically, until the smallest are thrown out.
scale: HH 24 lies some 1,300 light-years away, according to the International Gemini Observatory.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with GMOS on Gemini North through hydrogen-alpha and sulfur (S II) filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate particular red glows from hydrogen and sulfur, highlighting jets that would be hard to pick out by eye.

explore: The bright, nebulous star to the south is SSV 59, a visible T Tauri star. The busy environment around the core may also explain why some of the region's lowest-mass stars have been expelled.
alt: A reddish cloud with several narrow jets of gas streaming outward and a bright nebulous star to the south.
